Lipid drug-target genes & dementia risk — a two-sample MR reproduction

GLGC (exposure) × FinnGen (outcome), with an OpenGWAS extension

Workshop tutorial

2026-09-02

What this is. A workshop reproduction of the two-sample Mendelian randomization (2SMR) arm of Nordestgaard et al., Alzheimer’s & Dementia 2025 — do genetically-proxied lower non-HDL cholesterol, via six lipid drug-target genes, reduce dementia risk?

What this is not. Not the paper’s exact numbers, and not its one-sample / Cox arms. We use only the two no-request public datasets (GLGC lipids = exposure; FinnGen dementia and ischemic heart disease (IHD) = outcome). See plan.md and research.md.

1 The paper’s headline result (not ours)

paper1 <- rbindlist(list(
  data.table(outcome="dementia_all", gene=gene_order,
    or=c(0.24,0.18,0.97,1.66,1.41,0.30), lo=c(0.18,0.12,0.70,0.52,0.63,0.26), hi=c(0.31,0.25,1.35,5.36,3.16,0.34)),
  data.table(outcome="ihd", gene=gene_order,
    or=c(0.49,0.40,0.61,0.27,0.27,0.44), lo=c(0.42,0.33,0.51,0.13,0.17,0.40), hi=c(0.59,0.50,0.73,0.59,0.43,0.48))))
paper1[, outcome := factor(OUT_LAB[outcome], levels = OUT_LAB[c("dementia_all","ihd")])]
forest(paper1, "Paper's one-sample MR (NOT reproducible here)",
       sub = "Copenhagen + UK Biobank, individual-level data",
       xlab = "Odds ratio per 1 mmol/L lower non-HDL (log scale)", facet = "outcome")

The paper’s ONE-SAMPLE MR results (Copenhagen + UK Biobank individual-level data), per 1 mmol/L lower non-HDL. We could NOT reproduce these — shown for context. NOTE the unit differs from our per-SD two-sample estimates, so magnitudes are not directly comparable; compare directions only.

Genetically lower non-HDL cholesterol acting through HMGCR (the statin target), NPC1L1 (ezetimibe) and CETP carries roughly 70–80% lower odds of dementia — large effects with tight intervals, in the very targets already known to protect against heart disease. That is the paper’s strongest result, and it comes from its one-sample arm: ~500,000 people with genotypes, lipids and outcomes all measured in the same individuals. That data is application-gated and, for Copenhagen, legally unshareable, so the figure above is the paper’s published numbers, not ours — the headline we set out to chase and could not run (see why). Everything below is the two-sample arm that public summary statistics do support; note it is scaled per 1 SD rather than per 1 mmol/L, so compare directions, not magnitudes.

2 What is Mendelian randomization?

Observational studies can only show that low cholesterol and low dementia risk travel together; they can’t tell apart cause, reverse causation, and confounding. Mendelian randomization (MR) gets at causation by using genetic variants as a natural experiment. Because alleles are allocated randomly at conception — independently of lifestyle, wealth, or later illness — a variant that nudges a trait up or down acts like a lifelong, randomized “assignment” to more or less of that exposure. Such a variant, used as a genetic stand-in for the exposure, is called an instrument (or instrumental variable) — the tool the analysis leans on in place of a randomized treatment. If variants that lower non-HDL via a drug-target gene also lower dementia risk, that is causal evidence for inhibiting that target.

MR rests on three instrument assumptions: (1) relevance — the variant really affects the exposure (we check F ≫ 10); (2) independence — no confounding of the variant–outcome link; (3) exclusion restriction — the variant affects the outcome only through the exposure (we probe this with pleiotropy tests). Using cis variants inside the drug-target gene keeps the instrument tightly tied to that one protein, which is what makes it a good model of the drug.

2.1 One-sample vs two-sample MR

The estimate is essentially a ratio, (SNP→outcome) ÷ (SNP→exposure), and the two associations can come from the same people or from two different studies:

One-sample vs two-sample MR
Feature One-sample MR Two-sample MR
SNP→exposure and SNP→outcome measured in… the same individuals two different studies
Data needed individual-level genotypes + lipids + outcome published summary statistics only
Access application / restricted free download
This paper’s arms Copenhagen (CCHS+CGPS), UK Biobank GLGC × {FinnGen, UKB, Copenhagen}
Reproducible here? No Yes (GLGC × FinnGen)

Two-sample MR is what public data allows — we only ever need each variant’s published β and SE, not the raw participants. That single fact defines the whole scope of this reproduction (see why we did not reproduce the one-sample arm).

3 The design in one paragraph

For each of six targets — HMGCR (statins), NPC1L1 (ezetimibe), PCSK9, ANGPTL4, LPL, CETP — we take cis instrument SNPs, read their lipid effect from GLGC and their disease effect from FinnGen, harmonize to a common allele, and form the MR ratio (Wald ratio for 1 SNP; weighted median for ≥3). IHD is the positive control: a well-established effect of anti-atherogenic targets that must appear before we trust the dementia estimates. All effects are per 1 SD lower non-HDL.

pe   <- rd("mr_phase2_point_estimates.csv")
est  <- rd("mr_phase2_estimators.csv")
diag <- rd("mr_phase2_diagnostics.csv")
dn   <- rd("instruments_denovo.csv")
ad   <- rd("mr_phase3_ad_multisource.csv")
meta <- rd("mr_phase3_meta.csv")
main <- pe[exposure_trait == "nonHDL"]

4 Positive control: does IHD behave?

ihd <- main[outcome == "ihd" & !is.na(or)]
prot <- ihd[gene %in% c("HMGCR","LPL","PCSK9","CETP") & or < 1, gene]
cat(sprintf("**Anti-atherogenic targets protective for IHD (OR<1):** %s — %s\n",
            paste(prot, collapse = ", "),
            if (length(prot) >= 3) "**positive control PASSES**, so the dementia estimates are interpretable."
            else "**CHECK harmonization.**"))

Anti-atherogenic targets protective for IHD (OR<1): HMGCR, PCSK9, LPL, CETP — positive control PASSES, so the dementia estimates are interpretable.

5 Reproduction vs the paper — the two-sample arm

The fair comparison is our 2SMR against the paper’s 2SMR (both per 1 SD lower non-HDL). Rather than tabulate mostly-null numbers, we plot them side by side for the two outcomes the paper reports per target. Points left of 1 = protective.

paper2 <- rbindlist(list(
  data.table(outcome="dementia_all", gene=gene_order,
    or=c(0.59,0.43,1.03,1.08,1.60,0.54), lo=c(0.35,0.14,0.90,0.50,1.01,0.37), hi=c(0.99,1.33,1.17,2.32,2.55,0.78)),
  data.table(outcome="ihd", gene=gene_order,
    or=c(0.41,0.65,0.63,0.23,0.48,0.49), lo=c(0.30,0.34,0.58,0.15,0.37,0.40), hi=c(0.55,1.23,0.68,0.36,0.62,0.60))))
paper2[, series := "Paper 2SMR (also UKB+Copenhagen)"]
ours2 <- main[outcome %in% c("dementia_all","ihd"), .(outcome, gene, or, lo=or_lci, hi=or_uci)][, series := "This reproduction (FinnGen)"]
cmp <- rbind(paper2, ours2)[!is.na(or)]
cmp[, outcome := factor(OUT_LAB[outcome], levels = OUT_LAB[c("dementia_all","ihd")])]
forest(cmp, "Two-sample MR: reproduction vs paper", colour = "series", facet = "outcome")

Two-sample MR, per 1 SD lower non-HDL: this reproduction (GLGC×FinnGen) vs the paper’s meta-analyzed 2SMR (which also pooled UK Biobank + Copenhagen). Direction agrees for all six targets; our dementia estimates are attenuated toward the null, CETP most of all.

Reading it. For IHD the two series sit almost on top of each other (near-exact reproduction of the positive control). For all-cause dementia the directions match everywhere, but our CIs are wider and shrink toward the null — expected, because our outcome is FinnGen alone (~19k dementia cases) while the paper’s 2SMR pooled UKB + Copenhagen too. Note NPC1L1 and PCSK9 were also non-significant in the paper’s 2SMR. The largest gap is CETP — same protective direction, but attenuated from the paper’s 0.54 to 0.84 and no longer significant. Since our CETP→IHD matches the paper closely, that attenuation points at the FinnGen dementia outcome rather than the instrument.

subd <- main[outcome %in% c("ad","vascular","unspecified") & !is.na(or), .(outcome, gene, or, lo=or_lci, hi=or_uci)]
subd[, outcome := factor(OUT_LAB[outcome], levels = OUT_LAB[c("ad","vascular","unspecified")])]
forest(subd, "Dementia subtypes (this reproduction)", facet = "outcome")

Our dementia-subtype estimates (FinnGen only; the paper reported subtypes in its Figure 4). Wide CIs reflect small case counts (~6k AD, ~2.7k vascular, ~4.4k unspecified).

6 Robustness (Phase 2)

Target-specific exposures. Re-running each target on the trait it primarily acts on (LDL for the LDL-lowering targets, logTG for ANGPTL4/LPL) leaves directions unchanged; for the single-SNP Wald targets the p-value is invariant to the exposure trait (only the OR rescales).

Estimator agreement (PCSK9, CETP). All five estimators — IVW, weighted median, weighted mode, simple mode, MR-Egger — agree within rounding for both multi-SNP genes; MR-Egger is appropriately unstable at 3 SNPs (very wide CIs) and is shown for completeness rather than inference.

Assumption checks. Pleiotropy and heterogeneity are clean except a mild PCSK9→IHD Q signal:

if (nrow(diag)) show(diag, c("gene","outcome","n_snp","egger_intercept","egger_intercept_p","Q","Q_pval"),
  "MR-Egger intercept ≈ 0 (P>0.05) → little directional pleiotropy; Cochran's Q P>0.05 → no excess heterogeneity")

De-novo instrument selection. Replacing the hardcoded rsIDs with the paper’s method (cis window → GWAS-significant → LD-clump r²≤0.05 on a local 1000G EUR panel → F>10): every paper-named SNP is a genuine GWAS-significant cis variant (named_sig = named_n for all six); some survive as clump leads, others are absorbed into a stronger-lead clump. The de-novo MR agrees in direction with the curated instruments, and IHD stays protective.

if (nrow(dn)) show(dn, c("gene","n_cand","n_clumped","named_n","named_sig","named_lead","note"),
                   "De-novo selection vs the paper's named instruments")

7 Extension: bigger AD GWAS via OpenGWAS (NOT reproduction)

⚠ Bellenguez 2022 and Kunkle 2019 were not used by the original authors. This asks a different, stronger question — does the GLGC→AD signal hold in larger, independent AD GWAS? — and is reported separately from the reproduction.

adp <- ad[!is.na(or), .(gene, series = source, or, lo = or_lci, hi = or_uci)]
adp[, series := factor(series, levels = c("FinnGen R12","Kunkle 2019","Bellenguez 2022"))]
forest(adp, "AD by outcome source (extension)", colour = "series")

Alzheimer’s disease, per 1 SD lower non-HDL, by outcome GWAS. Precision grows with case count (FinnGen ~6k → Kunkle ~22k → Bellenguez ~39k+proxy). 

if (nrow(meta)) show(orci(meta), c("gene","k_sources","OR (95% CI)","pval","Q_pval","sources"),
  "Meta-analysis: FinnGen + Bellenguez (fixed-effect). Kunkle NOT pooled — Bellenguez already contains the Kunkle/IGAP samples.")

Adding cases sharpened the AD arm: the null targets became confident nulls (PCSK9 meta 1.02 (0.93–1.13)), and ANGPTL4 crossed into significance (harmful direction, consistent across all three GWAS). But ANGPTL4 remains single-instrument, so precision — not validity — is what improved; its OR is also scale-sensitive. Treat it as a lead for a multi-instrument follow-up, not a finding.

Where the sources disagree, there are concrete reasons — it is not random noise between equals. The sharpest example is HMGCR: protective/null in FinnGen (0.71) and Bellenguez (0.96) but significantly harmful in Kunkle (2.47, p=0.04). Two structural explanations, not biology:

  1. Single-instrument fragility. HMGCR, NPC1L1, ANGPTL4 and LPL each rest on one variant (a Wald ratio), so a cohort’s estimate is entirely that SNP’s association with AD in that dataset — there is no averaging to damp sampling noise, and a single-SNP estimate can flip sign between cohorts by chance. The multi-SNP genes (PCSK9, CETP) are correspondingly stable across all three sources. So a lone-SNP flip like HMGCR-in-Kunkle is expected imprecision, not a real contradiction.
  2. Different AD phenotypes. FinnGen is registry-diagnosed (Finnish ICD codes); Kunkle is clinically-adjudicated case–control; Bellenguez adds by-proxy cases (UK Biobank participants labelled by family history, not their own diagnosis). Proxy-AD is a noisier, diluted phenotype, so systematic gaps between Bellenguez and FinnGen partly reflect what “AD” means in each study, not just sample size. This is also why we lean on the FinnGen+Bellenguez meta (whose Cochran’s Q shows no significant disagreement) rather than any single source.

8 Why we did not reproduce the one-sample arm

One-sample MR needs individual-level data — every participant’s genotype and lipids and dementia status in one dataset — which exists only in Copenhagen (CCHS+CGPS; Danish law forbids public sharing) and UK Biobank (application required). Public summary statistics give only per-variant β/SE, which support two-sample MR but not one-sample. So the one-sample arm is permanently out of reach here; the paper’s published one-sample results are the headline figure at the top of this report.

That arm is where the paper’s dementia conclusions are strongest — HMGCR, NPC1L1, and CETP are clearly protective with tight intervals — because ~500k individuals and a per-mmol/L contrast give far more power than our single FinnGen summary dataset. Our two-sample arm reproduces the direction of these, and matches the well-powered IHD control closely, but cannot on its own deliver the same dementia significance.

9 Documented deviations from the paper

  • Outcome = FinnGen only (no UK Biobank / Copenhagen) → wider CIs, attenuated dementia effects.
  • Per 1 SD lower exposure (GLGC betas are per-SD), not the one-sample arm’s per 1 mmol/L.
  • logTG sensitivity reported per-SD, not per-halving of triglycerides.
  • De-novo instrument selection not re-run in the latest pass (needs the local 1000G LD panel).
  • Phase 3 uses AD GWAS the authors did not use — an extension, reported separately.
